label: 問8
source: AI-generated original. Common Test-style practice; no exam text reproduced.
passageHtml:
Essay Task: Public Spaces and Digital Technology

Step 1: Read several opinions. Step 2: Decide your position. Step 3: use Sources A and B to create an essay outline.

Step 1 - Opinions

Keiko (community nurse): Free public Wi-Fi can help people contact services, study, and receive emergency information. However, digital access should not replace staff who can assist residents face to face.

Martin (shop owner): Interactive signs bring more visitors to local areas. Small businesses benefit when people can discover events and routes in several languages.

Nora (privacy researcher): Sensors that count visitors may improve planning, but systems should collect the minimum data needed. People should know what is recorded and how long it is kept.

Owen (park designer): Technology can make parks more accessible through audio guides and navigation support. Yet screens should not dominate spaces intended for rest, conversation, and contact with nature.

Priya (student): Charging points and online booking make public facilities easier to use. Still, a person without a modern phone should be able to enter a library, reserve a room, or join an activity.

Step 2 - Your Position

Position: Cities should use digital technology in public spaces, but access and privacy protections must be built into the design.

Source A - A City Pilot Program

Westbridge installed multilingual digital kiosks in six parks. The kiosks displayed maps, event schedules, and emergency notices. To avoid excluding residents, each kiosk stood beside a printed map and included a large physical help button connected to the city information desk. After six months, requests for directions at nearby shops fell by 28%, while attendance at community events increased by 17%. The city did not require users to create accounts.

Source B - Visitor Survey

FeatureUnder 3030-5960+
Digital maps were useful88%79%61%
Printed maps should remain42%68%86%
Concerned about data collection54%63%71%
Would use a physical help button37%52%78%

Essay Outline

Reason 1: Technology can improve access to information.

Reason 2: Inclusive design should provide non-digital alternatives.

Reason 3: Privacy rules are necessary for public trust.

Additional Details from the Speakers

Keiko: During a recent heat wave, public Wi-Fi allowed residents to receive cooling-center updates. Several older residents still came to the community desk because they wanted confirmation from a person. To her, resilience means providing more than one route to essential information.

Martin: His shop joined a digital walking route created by the city. Visitors who would not normally enter the side street discovered local cafés and workshops. He supports the system because participation was optional and the city supplied printed route cards as well.

Nora: She distinguishes anonymous counting from personal tracking. A sensor that records how many people enter a park may be useful, but linking movement to individual phones creates a different level of risk. She recommends short retention periods, independent audits, and notices written in ordinary language.

Owen: He has designed audio descriptions for people with visual impairments and vibration alerts near construction zones. He also removes screens from quiet garden areas. Good design, he argues, begins with the purpose of the space rather than with the newest available device.

Priya: At her university, study rooms can be reserved online, but two rooms remain available without reservations. This mixed system is less efficient on paper, yet it protects students whose phones are broken, whose data plans have ended, or who need help from staff.

Source C - Proposed City Principles

  1. Provide a clear public benefit before collecting any data.
  2. Keep a non-digital option for essential services.
  3. Explain data collection at the point of use.
  4. Test systems with residents of different ages and abilities.
  5. Review whether the technology still serves its original purpose after one year.

The proposal notes that inclusion is not achieved simply by installing accessible hardware. Instructions, staff training, maintenance, and the cost of personal devices can all affect whether residents are truly able to use a service.

questions.question: Which option best summarizes Keiko's opinion?
options: Digital services should completely replace public employees.
Public Wi-Fi is useful, but human assistance should remain.
Emergency information should be available only on phones.
Residents should pay for access to online services.
questions.answer: Public Wi-Fi is useful, but human assistance should remain.
questions.evidence: digital access should not replace staff
questions.reason_ja: 利便性を認めつつ対面支援を残す立場です。

questions.question: Which two speakers most clearly stress that technology should not remove existing forms of access?
options: Keiko and Priya
Martin and Nora
Nora and Owen
Martin and Owen
questions.evidence: should not replace staff ... person without a modern phone should be able
questions.reason_ja: 対面支援とスマホなしの利用を守る二人です。

questions.question: Which shared idea best supports the stated position?
options: Technology should be introduced without limits.
Digital systems are valuable only for younger residents.
Benefits should be combined with protections against exclusion or misuse.
Printed information should replace all digital tools.
questions.answer: Benefits should be combined with protections against exclusion or misuse.
questions.evidence: access and privacy protections must be built into the design
questions.reason_ja: 立場の中心は利点と保護策の両立です。

questions.question: What is the best use of Source A in the essay?
options: To show that digital kiosks can improve information access while preserving alternatives
To prove that printed maps are never used
To argue that every public service should require an account
To demonstrate that local shops lose visitors after kiosks are installed
questions.answer: To show that digital kiosks can improve information access while preserving alternatives
questions.evidence: printed map ... physical help button ... attendance increased
questions.reason_ja: 効果と非デジタル代替の両方を示します。

questions.question: Which statement is best supported by Source B?
options: Older visitors were the least interested in physical help.
All age groups opposed printed maps.
Support for keeping printed maps increased with age.
Privacy concern was highest among people under 30.
questions.answer: Support for keeping printed maps increased with age.
questions.reason_ja: 年齢層が上がるほど紙地図を残す支持が高まっています。

questions.question: Which evidence best supports Reason 3 about privacy?
options: Attendance at events rose by 17%.
Requests for directions fell by 28%.
Concern about data collection exceeded half in every age group.
Digital maps were useful to 88% of people under 30.
questions.answer: Concern about data collection exceeded half in every age group.
questions.reason_ja: 全世代で半数超がデータ収集を懸念しています。

questions.question: Which conclusion best fits the completed outline?
options: Cities should reject technology because some residents prefer paper.
Cities should use technology only for commercial advertising.
Well-designed public technology can help people when it remains inclusive and transparent.
Digital systems are successful only when they collect personal accounts.
questions.answer: Well-designed public technology can help people when it remains inclusive and transparent.
questions.reason_ja: 包摂性と透明性を備えた導入という結論です。
